title: 17 years a programmer — this time I didn't write a single line myself. My AI-only workflow, 5 months in
author: DaedalusR8
selftext:
Campaign Forge is an Infinite Story RPG I've been developing solo since March — an AI co-author builds a chapter-by-chapter campaign around the party you create, on top of a full tactical RPG in Godot (grid combat plus a big in-game creation suite).

I've programmed for 17 years, and for this project I decided to leave every single code change to Claude (Opus 4.6 through 4.8, Fable when available) — mostly with great success. My job is everything that is NOT writing code: I lead the design, review everything, playtest extensively, and write very picky bug reports.

Two rules made it work. First, whenever I wanted to make a code change myself, I prompted my reasoning to Claude instead and asked whether my thinking was correct or whether better alternatives existed — when it claimed one did, we discussed it and decided together. Second, Claude writes all project documentation at every step, which doubles as its own long-term memory.

Not everything worked. We once templated NPC dialogue to save tokens on small local models and it flattened every character into the same voice — reverted, lesson learned. What DID work for weak models was flipping the direction: instead of the AI inventing structure from scratch, the code picks one hand-authored template from a moddable pool and the AI improves it. Strong models get a line telling them they may ignore the template entirely.

That matters because the game ships with a local AI inside it (llama.cpp + a small Qwen model) — campaigns generate fully offline, no account, no API key.

Trailer: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7AxeDs-T0dU](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7AxeDs-T0dU)  
Steam: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4918080](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4918080)

Happy to answer anything about the workflow — what broke, how the docs-as-memory setup works, or what reviewing 100% AI-written code for five months does to your brain.

comments.author: Intelligent-Neat9974
comments.body:
How do you handle the dialog system. I assume the small ai models help, but do you find it struggles maintaining relationships between NPCs, locations, events, etc. when building out the stories?
No plans for localization?

replies.author: DaedalusR8
replies.body:
Dialogue is its own focused generation step, not part of one big story call. Chapter generation is a staged pipeline: world database first (characters, factions, regions, enemies — all with stable IDs), then the chapter outline, then scenes, then dialogue per scene as small calls with narrow JSON schemas. Small models do far better on many small constrained calls than on one giant "write me a chapter" prompt.

The relationship problem is real, and my answer became: never ask the model to remember anything. The world database is the single source of truth, and every call gets fed exactly the slice of it that call needs. Things that happen in play — oaths, deaths, betrayals — get written into a memory store, and the next chapter's prompts have to honor those entries as canon. Then AFTER generation, code enforces referential integrity: every NPC referenced in a scene has to resolve against the database. If a small model invents a character mid-scene, the pipeline synthesizes a real NPC record for it instead of failing; if it reuses an existing ID for something new, the reference gets de-conflicted and repaired. So the model is only ever creative inside a frame, and the frame is code.

What small models still struggle with is flavor, not structure — that's where the template pools from the post come in. Structure from code, flavor from the model, validation to catch what falls through. On the bundled 4B model stories come out simpler but complete and playable; on a bigger local model they get genuinely good capability wise (I still have to tune).

Localization: nothing promised for the EA launch - English only \_for now\_. It's an interesting problem for a generated game though, because the translation would happen at generation time rather than in string tables, and the schemas/vocab the models are validated against are all English today. I'm German myself, so it's genuinely on my mind, but I only announce what's built.

replies.author: TheSpanxxx
replies.body: I love this. How are you handling bloat? Have you run some math in db size projections? I'm curious if the game were heavily played what your table growth looks like.

replies.author: DaedalusR8
replies.body:
There's no database in the SQL sense and nothing global that grows. Each campaign is its own folder of JSON files, because everything the AI generates is structured text — maps, scenes, dialogue trees, memory entries. Art and audio are shipped assets referenced by ID.

Measured across months of test campaigns: world creation writes \~1.5–3 MB once (almost all of it pre-baked region tilemaps), then each generated chapter adds roughly 0.9 MB — nearly all of that the full chapter file, which I keep on purpose so any past chapter stays replayable. The part people expect to bloat — the AI's long-term story memory — is the smallest thing on disk: after a few chapters the whole memory folder is about 6 KB, because it stores typed facts ("oath sworn", "villain escaped"), not transcripts. So a 20-chapter campaign lands around 20 MB currently.

replies.author: promptling
replies.body: Before the public build, I’d define one 15-minute path: create a party, use the G.O.D. menu, finish one combat, and read the generated aftermath. Then ask exactly where context was lost and whether the chapter felt internally consistent. I’m building [Patchloop](https://patchloop.io/) for unfinished AI-built games and structured feedback loops; Campaign Forge would be a fascinating project to follow there.

comments.author: fnwc
comments.body: I’ve thought about doing this for the SRD for 3rd edition D&D. Using an AI to generate “choose your own adventure style “ interactions by reading a module or ad hoc and generating a strongly typed framework rather than ad libbed on the fly.

replies.author: DaedalusR8
replies.body:
That "strongly typed framework rather than ad-libbed" instinct is exactly where I landed. Generation happens up front into typed, validated data - scenes, dialogue trees, encounters as JSON against schemas - and play mostly just consumes that data.  
  
Reading an existing module into the typed frame is a nice variant of the same shape - I generate my world database from scratch, but ingestion into the same kind of structure should work. If you build it for the 3e SRD I'd genuinely like to see it.

comments.author: TheBinkz
comments.body:
Hey thanks for sharing. Im kinda in the same boat. Just starting out and wanting to make a game for me and my daughter to play. 

Hooked up the MCP connection to unity which took way longer than it should have. Tested it by asking it to make a simple black box at 0,0 and it did a bunch of extra stuff that it probably should not have. Some of which isn't even required.

My question, how do you translate what you want into the prompt so that its done correctly? Not even a prompt related to unity per se. But in general.

replies.author: DaedalusR8
replies.body:
I try to always give examples to the AI of what I mean, and when it's an "unfinished idea" I make sure to write that in the prompt aswell. I ask the AI to audit the existing Codebase a lot, and \*always\* invite per prompt to freely ask any Questions it has. If I am uncertain the AI "gets it", I ask it to explain in detail what I want it to do next, from its own view.

If what the AI describes seems correct, we can proceed.

One thing I keep forgetting to mention in other replies: Always make a multi stage Plan \_and save it\_ before starting new implementations, unless its a bugfix, small value changes for configurations, etc.

I use an [overview.md](http://overview.md) that links to all other documentation in the project, and starts with some "hard rules" at the top. After every single Compaction I manually insert my Refresh-and-Reanchor-Block, where links to directly useful information, the [overview.md](http://overview.md) and other relevant files are written down.

comments.author: Time_Cat_5212
comments.body:
I'm curious: Many critics of AI-assisted software development lean heavily on the idea of experienced programmers who know how to write code (real engineers) versus noobs trying to vibe their way to success.  I have my own opinions about this as a noob using AI tools and taking specs and code quality seriously, but I want to hear yours as someone with real experience.

You wrote code for 17 years.  What's your take on this?  How did your experience shape your workflow with AI tools?  Why did you decide to rely entirely on AI to write ALL the code even when you presumably have the skills to do a lot of it yourself?  With your seasoned eye, what do you think of the code it wrote?  What was your input like, and how did you manage the quality of the output?

replies.author: DaedalusR8
replies.body:
The reason I decided to completely make every code change through the AI was so the Documentation \*always\* reflects the exact state of the Project. And every connected site, be it in code or in documentation, will be extended as needed aswell. Human-Programmers just will not do that in many cases, and that has led to an incredible amount of mistakes that were completely and utterly avoidable in my past and the past of IT as a whole. I myself always praise documentation and doing the documenting, but I \*will\* forget to do it at times, and that has \*always\* gone bad. With a Project of this size, the first big project decision was to swallow my pride and accept that the project will fail if I try to do this myself without the use of AI and the technology many brilliant people have worked on for the betterment of Technology as a whole. 

  
I told Claude: "You're the logical mind of this Project, and you are the Lead Developer. If you think what I am trying to do is bad, tell me freely. Ask Questions if anything is unclear to you" and reminded it again when it seemed to forget that.

I raged several times at being corrected for things I was certain would be the exact right solution for the problem I'm seeing at the moment; I had solved such things dozens of times before and I was certain it was THE solution. The AI was still right 90% of the Time and I delayed the project by insisting on myself. It's a simple mismatch of knowledge, I just dont have access to the amount of Information the AI does in every single area. No matter how much I may know about my field of experience, I don't know how well my Knowledge and Ideas combine and mesh with Information outside of my view. By doing a general research pass before big implementations, with the help of AI and through AI, I dramatically expand my possibilities.

The 10% of times it was wrong and I accepted that were dangerous, and I'm glad other Technology like Git existed in those times.

  
Making Fire with Firestones will never be a bad skill to have. That foundational knowledge can be combined with other knowledge to create even more Technology, we've always done that. But Lighters do exists.

  
To the Code it writes: That depends on what you set up during Project Planning, if you tell your AI of choice (and keep telling them) to build modular and describe what you mean with some examples (2+ are optimal, with two examples AI can analyze both and make more examples for itself to solidify the Schema logically; more are better, I usually use 2 examples still).

"Good Code" and "Bad Code" has always be subjective, as I experienced it so far people mostly complain about not being able to read code of some kind (me included often enough). If you plan and work with a good code structure, you usually can't have Bad Code -> you'd have errors or warnings then.

  
Having started as a programmer was very good experience for starting with AI-Development, Code-wise I believe Programmers working with AI will have better results working on Code than Visual Artists working on Code with AI, unless speed is traded for research as needed; Visual Artists working on visual media with AI will get better results for visual media than programmers working on visual media with AI, unless speed is traded for research as needed. And so on.

replies.author: fnwc
replies.body:
I’ve come across the same. I use actual tests/locks to prevent documentation (Md) drift. I have an enormous amount of tests and tooling built to lock in the desired infrastructure and am constantly asking, “how do we prevent this bug from happening in the future”.  ADRs etc provide a lot here. 

I’m a former developer as well. I view AI as another tool. I think people ignore the fact that people have the same context drift as AI.
